title: What naḥw is
summary: Naḥw is the science of the Arabic sentence: how words join, which words govern others, and why each word ends as it does.

sections.heading: The science of the sentence
paragraphs: Naḥw studies the word inside the sentence. It asks what role a word plays, which other word governs it, and what ending that role gives it. The classical books call it the science of the states of the endings of words, in iʿrāb and bināʾ.

Its first question is the division of the word into noun, verb and particle. From there it moves to the four states of iʿrāb, the nominal and the verbal sentence, and the words that change the ending of others.

sections.heading: Why it is studied
paragraphs: The books give naḥw a plain aim: to keep the tongue from error and to understand the Qurʾān, the Sunna and the books of the scholars. In the madrasa it is an instrument (āla): a science learnt for the sake of the sciences it opens.

The tradition traces its first rules to Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī in Basra. Sībawayh's al-Kitāb, written in the second/eighth century, is its first great book; later teachers wrote the short handbooks that students still memorise, such as al-Ājurrūmiyya.
